content:
# Disagreement Log — 1 Maccabees Chapter 8

**Date:** 2026-03-17
**Translators:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA

---

## Summary
Total disagreements: 31

---

## Disagreement Entries

**1MA 8:1 — "accepted all who came to them" vs. "welcomed all who joined them"**
- EMET: "accepted all who came to them"
- LOGOS: "welcomed all who joined them"
- PNEUMA: "welcome all who come to them"
- RULING: "welcomed all who came to them" — LOGOS/PNEUMA; *prosedechonto* = received/welcomed; "accepted" (EMET) is slightly passive

**1MA 8:1 — "made a league of friendship" vs. "established treaties of friendship"**
- EMET: "made a league of friendship"
- LOGOS: "established treaties of friendship"
- PNEUMA: "make alliances and treaties"
- RULING: "made treaties of friendship" — *ephilopoiesanto* + *sunthekas* = friendship-treaties; "league" is archaic; "treaties" is standard

**1MA 8:2 — "brave deeds" vs. "brave deeds they had performed"**
- Minor variation. All translators agree on substance. "Brave deeds" adopted.

**1MA 8:2 — "conquered them and brought them under tribute" vs. "conquered the Galatians and made them subject to tribute"**
- EMET: "conquered them and brought them under tribute"
- LOGOS: "conquered the Galatians and made them subject to tribute"
- RULING: LOGOS; specifying "Galatians" avoids ambiguity at this point in the narrative

**1MA 8:3 — "mines of silver and of gold" vs. "silver and gold mines"**
- EMET: "mines of silver and of gold"
- LOGOS/PNEUMA: "silver and gold mines"
- RULING: "silver and gold mines" — more natural English word order

**1MA 8:4 — "by their counsel and their patience" vs. "through careful planning and persistence"**
- EMET: "by their counsel and their patience"
- LOGOS: "through careful planning and persistence"
- PNEUMA: "through planning and persistence"
- RULING: "through planning and persistence" — *boule* = planning/counsel; *makrothumia* = long-suffering/persistence; LOGOS formulation with PNEUMA simplification

**1MA 8:4 — "kings who came from the end of the earth against them they crushed and struck"**
- EMET: "kings who came from the end of the earth against them they crushed and struck"
- LOGOS: "They had crushed the kings who came against them from the ends of the earth, inflicted severe defeats"
- RULING: LOGOS; more natural syntax

**1MA 8:5 — "vanquished and brought under their power" vs. "defeated and brought under their control"**
- EMET: "vanquished and brought under their power"
- LOGOS: "defeated and brought under their control"
- RULING: "defeated and brought under their authority" — "authority" for *exousia* is more precise than "control" or "power"

**1MA 8:6 — "with a hundred and twenty elephants" — all agree**
- All translators preserve the number. No disagreement.

**1MA 8:6 — "he too had been defeated" — passive vs. "he was defeated"**
- Minor variation. "He too was defeated" (LOGOS) preferred.

**1MA 8:7 — "took him alive" — all agree**
- All translators preserve "took him alive." No disagreement. Historically: the Romans did not literally capture Antiochus III; they defeated him at Magnesia (190 BCE). The author oversimplifies. Translators do not correct.

**1MA 8:7 — "a parcel of land" vs. "substantial territory"**
- EMET: "a parcel of land"
- LOGOS: "substantial territory"
- RULING: "a parcel of their territory" — *eparchia* is a province/territory; "substantial" (LOGOS) adds an interpretation; "parcel" (EMET) is too small-sounding

**1MA 8:8 — "fairest lands of his" vs. "finest lands"**
- EMET: "fairest lands"
- LOGOS: "finest lands"
- RULING: "finest lands" — *beltiston* = best/finest; "fairest" is ambiguous

**1MA 8:9 — "men of Greece had taken counsel to come and destroy them"**
- EMET: "men of Greece had taken counsel"
- LOGOS: "The Greeks had once devised a plan"
- RULING: "The Greeks had once plotted to come and destroy them" — LOGOS; "plotted" is more accurate to the political conspiracy

**1MA 8:10 — "the matter was made known to them" vs. "the Romans got word of it" vs. "the Romans learned of it"**
- EMET: "the matter was made known to them"
- LOGOS: "the Romans learned of it"
- PNEUMA: "The Romans got wind of it"
- RULING: "But the Romans got word of it" — PNEUMA; appropriately active; "got word" is natural and not colloquial

**1MA 8:10 — "one of their captains" vs. "a single general"**
- EMET: "one of their captains"
- LOGOS: "a single general"
- PNEUMA: "one general"
- RULING: "a single commander" — balance between LOGOS's "general" and EMET's "captain"

**1MA 8:10 — "made slaves to this day" vs. "made subject to Rome — as they remain to this day"**
- EMET: "made them slaves to this day"
- LOGOS: "made subject to Rome — as they remain to this day"
- RULING: "reduced to subjection — as they remain to this day" — LOGOS; "slaves" is too strong; *hupotetaktas* = subjected/made subordinate

**1MA 8:11 — "destroyed and made slaves" vs. "destroyed or subjugated"**
- EMET: "they destroyed and made slaves"
- LOGOS: "they, too, were destroyed or subjugated"
- RULING: "likewise destroyed and made subject" — avoids the slavery language; "subject" is more precise

**1MA 8:12 — "relied on them" vs. "leaned on them" vs. "who depended on them"**
- EMET: "those who relied on them"
- LOGOS: "those who relied on them" (same)
- PNEUMA: "the allies who leaned on them"
- RULING: "those who relied on them" — EMET/LOGOS; straightforward

**1MA 8:13 — "those whom they wish to make kings" — all agree**
- All translators agree on this sentence about Roman power. No disagreement.

**1MA 8:14 — "to make themselves great" — all agree**
- The striking observation that no Roman wore a crown or purple robe — all translators recognize this as admiring and ironic. No disagreement on the substance.

**1MA 8:15 — "three hundred and twenty men" — all agree**
- All preserve the exact number. No disagreement. (Historically, the Senate had ~300 members; the text's 320 may be a textual variant or slight inaccuracy in the source.)

**1MA 8:15 — "deliberating always for the people" vs. "deliberating perpetually over public affairs"**
- EMET: "deliberating always for the people, to govern them well"
- LOGOS: "deliberating perpetually over public affairs, to govern the people well"
- RULING: LOGOS; "perpetually" is better than "always" for *aei*; "public affairs" is clearer than "for the people"

**1MA 8:16 — "entrust their government to one man every year"**
- All translators agree on this description of the Roman consulship (rendered as a single man). The text says "one man" and all preserve it. No disagreement.

**1MA 8:16 — "no envy or jealousy among them"**
- All translators agree on this idealized description. No disagreement.

**1MA 8:17 — "Eupolemus son of John, son of Accos" — names preserved**
- All translators preserve the genealogy exactly. No disagreement.

**1MA 8:18 — "lift the yoke from them" vs. "obtain relief from the yoke"**
- EMET: "to lift the yoke from them"
- LOGOS: "to obtain relief from the yoke"
- PNEUMA: "to get Israel out from under the Greek yoke"
- RULING: "to obtain relief from the yoke" — LOGOS; "lift" is literal but LOGOS's "obtain relief" is more idiomatic; PNEUMA's expansion ("get Israel out from under") is explanatory

**1MA 8:19 — "entered the senate house" — all agree**
- All translators preserve "senate house." No disagreement.

**1MA 8:20 — treaty enrollment language**
- EMET: "register us as your allies and friends"
- LOGOS: "enroll us among your allies and friends"
- PNEUMA: "be enrolled among your allies and friends"
- RULING: "enroll us among your allies and friends" — LOGOS; *sungraphesthai* = to register/enroll (in a formal list); "enroll" is the technical term

**1MA 8:22 — "bronze tablets" — all agree**
- The bronze tablet inscription is a historically accurate detail of Roman treaty practice. All translators preserve it. No disagreement.

**1MA 8:30 — "at their pleasure" vs. "at their own discretion"**
- EMET: "at their pleasure"
- LOGOS: "at their own discretion"
- RULING: "at their own discretion" — more appropriate for legal treaty language

**1MA 8:32 — "we will do judgment for them" vs. "we will take up their cause"**
- EMET: "we will do judgment for them"
- LOGOS: "we will take up their cause"
- PNEUMA: "we will take up their cause"
- RULING: "we will take up their cause" — LOGOS/PNEUMA; "do judgment" is archaic and imprecise; the Roman letter is offering advocacy and military action

**1MA 8:32 — "by sea and by land" — all agree**
- The formula is preserved by all. No disagreement.
